corrected_statement: Tuning candidates are chosen by the task's strictly proper primary (metrics.PRIMARY: squared error, log loss or ranked probability score) pooled over every inner validation row (sum of w*loss / sum of w, survey-weighted under the population answer, rounded to 1e-9 relative before the argmin), or, for a forest where every row is its own unit, folds do not follow time, the sample answer applies and no step reads the outcome, pooled over its out-of-bag predictions; never by an average of per-fold scores such as R-squared, and never by AUC or accuracy (tuning.Loss admits only mse/log_loss/rps; a task with no such loss, a time to event, cannot fit a tuned family).
source_note: All four internal rulings exist and say this: RECIPES_AND_TUNING.md §4.2 'Score' row (line 789), F5 (line 126: RidgeCV averages per-fold R², 'not the pooled primary score (ruling 4)'), §7.3 'Impossible by construction: tuning on AUC or accuracy' (line 1330); MODELING_SEQUENCE.md ruling 4 (line 65: 'Prediction selects and declares on a strictly proper score'). Ruling 4 gives a methods reason only by naming strict propriety (metrics.SEMI_PROPER cites Van Calster et al., STRATOS TG6, for AUC being semi-proper); pooling rather than averaging per-fold scores is stated as a decision with no cited methods reason. No literature (e.g. Gneiting & Raftery 2007) is cited for the tuning objective itself.
note: The inventory's cited test (test_tuning_plan.py::test_the_pooled_loss_is_the_weighted_mean_of_every_inner_rows_loss) checks only pooled_loss's arithmetic (weak). Two stronger tests exist: test_t3 recomputes each candidate's survey-weighted pooled inner MSE by hand with a direct sklearn HistGradientBoostingRegressor fit (no engine import for the loss) and matches record.losses to 1e-12; the elastic-net test recomputes the exact pooled curve, checks the choice is its rounded argmin, and asserts the fixture's per-fold-average choice differs. These certify what the app computes; that pooling a strictly proper loss is the right tuning objective is a sourced principle (proper scoring) plus a judgment (pooling over averaging), with nothing in the repo checking it. Corrected statement adds the forest out-of-bag exception (tuning.py:1737, RECIPES §4.2 'Forest, out of bag') and that time-to-event (brier_t not in Loss) refuses tuned families (pipeline.py:532).

source_note: No source at featurewise.py:209. The math layer it calls (models/inference.py:11-16) cites Bell & McCaffrey 2002 (Surv Methodol 28:169) for CR2 and Pustejovsky & Tipton 2018 (J Bus Econ Stat 36:672; verified on Crossref: 'Small-Sample Methods for Cluster-Robust Variance Estimation and Hypothesis Testing in Fixed Effects Models', 36(4):672-683) for the Satterthwaite/Bell-McCaffrey df; inference.py:646 cites Cameron & Miller for clustered SEs. That independence-based intervals are too narrow under positive within-unit correlation is standard (Moulton; Cameron & Miller) but is not cited here. The 200 cap (CR2_MAX_FEATURES, featurewise.py:61) is a compute limit with no methods basis, and the user text says so ('beyond what TurboTab computes').
note: Code matches: with clusters.clustered and m > 200 a refusal is built (featurewise.py:209-215), intervals/p/q are None and only point estimates are kept; at most 200 exposures each get CR2 by inference.cr2 with BM df. test_3b checks the clustered CR2 SE and df against references.cr2_by_definition (written-out matrices, numpy only, no engine import), and test_spec_curve.py::test_repeated_rows_give_cr2_intervals_as_clubsandwich_computes_them checks the math layer against clubSandwich. No test checks the >200 refusal: none references CR2_MAX_FEATURES or the refusal text. Minor: when Bell-McCaffrey df exceed BM_BUDGET, _cr2_tests falls back to t(G-1) (featurewise.py:291), yet the caption still says 'on t with Bell–McCaffrey degrees of freedom' (featurewise.py:261). The separate floor_refusal (too few clusters) also applies first.

source_note: The method (a whole-chain bootstrap's percentile interval; under imputation Schomaker & Heumann's Boot MI, eq. 3.5) is sourced in methods/calibration.py:55-73: Schomaker & Heumann 2018 (verified on Crossref: Stat Med 37:2252-2266, doi 10.1002/sim.7654) and Keogh, Shaw & Gustafson 2020 for refusing model-based SEs. The default of 200 (decisions.py:293, :622) has no source. MIN_BOOT_SHARE = 0.9 (stages/calibration.py:511-513) is labeled 'a stated floor' with a one-line reason ('past it the resamples left out would shape the interval'): a decision, not a sourced threshold. The drop-direction remark (calibration.py:1083-1088, 'REPAIR-RC') is a reasoned argument with no source. The app's own rule elsewhere cuts against 200: decisions.py:448 and methods/substitution.py:101-107 quote Carpenter & Bithell 2000 (verified on Crossref: Stat Med 19:1141-1164) that a percentile interval wants B of 1,000 to 2,000, and stages/modeling.py:43 uses a normal band at 200 for that reason.
note: Code matches: enough = n_ok >= 2 and n_ok >= 0.9*n_boot (calibration.py:1008); SE and CI are None when not enough; failed resamples of any kind (singular fit, not finite, imputation refused, no positive true-intake covariance) are left out, and the 'end away from zero may be too near' tail sentence is added only when some were CalibrationRefused. The known-truth simulation (200 datasets, Boot MI with 100 resamples, coverage >= 0.93, observed 0.945) would fail if the percentile interval undercovered at small B in that setting, so the interval's adequacy is certified there (univariate, persons resampled). The 200 default and the 90% floor are conventions; the 90% withholding branch has no test (no test checks the 'fewer than 90% ... no interval is shown' path; test_4_under_repeated_units only pins the 49-of-50 kept text). Sent to review because the app states two rules for a percentile interval's B: 1,000+ (Carpenter & Bithell, substitution and modeling) and 200 here. The ms5 simulation suggests 100-200 is adequate in this setting, so one of the two places should say why they differ.

source_note: No source is cited, and none is needed: this is a logic claim about the app's own code. The family's definition is in estimand.family_exposures (estimand.py:503) and quest.py:516 (the set_multiplicity declaration applies only when state.estimand.family is set). It holds in the code: set_multiplicity reaches results only through stages/effects.py:894-900 (_multiplicity, applied only to a tests-only family, i.e. feature-wise) and methods/omics.py:1719 apply_multiplicity, which only keeps or removes the Benjamini-Hochberg q column and rewrites the caption; it never alters a p-value or interval. FeatureWiseTests(features=exposures) tests only matrix columns named exactly as an exposure (featurewise.py:96-107, :355-358), so one exposure gives one test and BH's q equals p. Modifier heterogeneity tests are counted separately and reported unadjusted with the count stated (methods/interaction.py:195-225), whatever set_multiplicity says. Quintile and spline terms are never fed to apply_multiplicity.
test_judged: none found (no test references _multiplicity_changes or the 'one study factor' line)
note: The inventory's worry (that a single exposure still yields several tests the method acts on) does not hold: set_multiplicity acts only on the feature-wise table, which has one test per exposure column. The silencing is correct by code reading, but nothing pins it. Two side findings. (1) The opposite branch of the same check, sweep.py:190 ('Another way of accounting for the n tests changes their p-values and intervals'), overstates: no multiplicity method changes p-values or intervals; it changes only the q-values and the caption. (2) _multiplicity_changes counts every exposure-role column in state.roles, while the family is the settled exposure-role predictors (estimand.family_exposures), so the two counts can differ when an exposure-role column is not a predictor.

source_note: calm/FOUNDATION.md §5 rule 6 (line 336) says: 'No estimate and no score before Fit. Seeing estimates while choosing invites choosing by the estimate.' This is a ruling with a one-line methods reason. BLUEPRINT.md:453 places 'Which of my decisions mattered?' after the plan is locked. Gelman & Loken 2013 ('The garden of forking paths', 14 Nov 2013 technical report, fetched from sites.stat.columbia.edu and read from its text) contains the quoted forks: 'choices of control variables in a regression, transformations, and data coding and excluding rules'. Its argument is that data-contingent analysis choices invalidate nominal inference, and that the clean case is a preregistered choice. This supports sealing the curve until the plan is fixed. Gelman & Loken do not discuss specification curves, which come from Simonsohn, Simmons & Nelson 2020, cited in the module docstring; applying their argument to a curve is the app's own step.
note: Code matches: specification_curve returns a sealed SpecCurve with no specs and never calls fit unless is_lock(lock) (spec_curve.py:340-370), and SEALED is the user text. The named test is a real enforcement check: fit raises if it is called, and the test asserts calls == []. But it checks that the app enforces the rule, not the methods reason behind it, so it is weak for this claim. No test could certify the reason; it rests on the forking-paths argument.

corrected_statement: When the trial's logistic fit by Newton's method does not converge in 100 steps, gives a non-finite or singular step, ends with any |coefficient| > 25, or ends with any fitted risk within 1e-10 of 0 or 1 (all read as separation), the standardized risk difference and ratio are refused. The message says some group all had the event or none did, so the model's risk runs to 0% or 100% and no finite estimate exists.
source_note: No source at trials.py:715-751, the GEE path at :1136, or the methods docstring (trials.py:32-37, which cites Ye, Shao, Yi & Zhao 2023 and R's beeca for the standardized risks and their variance). Standard theory (e.g. Albert & Anderson 1984, not cited) shows the logistic coefficients' MLE does not exist under separation. It does not show the standardized (g-computation) risks lack a finite value: each is an average of bounded fitted risks, whose limit is finite. Only the log risk ratio diverges, and only when a whole arm's standardized risk goes to 0, i.e. no events in an arm.
note: The test sets every event to 1 in one site (a covariate stratum, not an arm) and asserts the refusal and its '0% or 100%' text. It checks the behavior, not that no finite estimate exists. In that exact fixture the standardized RD and RR have finite limits: site c's rows have risk 1 under both arms, and the arm contrast comes from the other sites. So the stated reason overstates. Refusing is a defensible conservative choice: the Ye et al. variance is built from the inverse information, which is near-singular, and the coefficients do diverge. But the wording should say the logistic model has no finite fit, so TurboTab does not report the standardized risks, rather than that no finite estimate exists. The numeric triggers (|beta| > 25, any fitted risk < 1e-10) can also fire on a strongly predictive covariate without exact separation, and the message still calls it separation. Note that R's beeca, the stated reference, would warn and still return an estimate here.

source_note: The cited source (models/causal.py:1159-1163) is Kutner, Nachtsheim & Neter 2004, Applied Linear Regression Models §10.5. That section is the multicollinearity diagnostic, where a maximum VIF above 10 is the customary sign that multicollinearity unduly influences least-squares estimates. This comes from the text's known content; the textbook could not be fetched and web search was exhausted. It supports R² ≥ 0.9 (VIF 10) as a conventional collinearity line. It does not treat positivity. Reading the threshold as a 'practical positivity violation' is the app's own step. A global cross-fitted R² does not show whether the exposure varies at every covariate pattern, which is what positivity for a continuous exposure requires (a positive conditional density). The code calls it 'the app's convention', and the inventory notes this too.
note: Code matches: variation() flags r2 >= CONTINUOUS_R2_LINE = 0.9 on the cross-fitted exposure model (causal.py:1176-1183). The fit stage withholds the estimate with _variation_reason unless spec.acknowledged (stages/causal.py:740-742). For a numeric exposure the only exit is 'Keep every row; record that positivity is practically violated' (core/causal.py:1072-1088; no trimming). The test recomputes the estimator's cross-fitted R² by hand (plr_by_hand) and checks the 409 refusal, the single acknowledged exit and the methods sentence. So the computation and the enforcement are real, but nothing checks that R² ≥ 0.9 marks a positivity problem. Suggested softening: present it as a convention borrowed from the collinearity rule (VIF 10) for how little of the exposure's own variation is left, not as a positivity criterion. The reason text also says 'revisit the adjustment set', which is offered as advice, not as an exit.

source_note: Verified on Europe PMC: Schmidt FL, Le H, Ilies R. 'Beyond alpha: an empirical examination of the effects of different sources of measurement error on reliability estimates for measures of individual differences constructs.' Psychol Methods 2003;8(2):206-224, doi 10.1037/1082-989x.8.2.206, PMID 12924815. The abstract says Cronbach's alpha 'fails to assess transient error' and produces 'overestimates of reliability and undercorrections for biases due to measurement error'. The paper discusses alpha; extending it to ω is a sound inference, since both are single-occasion internal-consistency coefficients. The same abstract says the coefficient of equivalence and stability is 'the only classical reliability coefficient assessing all three major sources of measurement error (random response, transient, and specific factor errors)'. So a same-form test-retest coefficient captures transient error, as claimed, but not specific-factor error, and it can also absorb true change over the interval. MODELING_SEQUENCE.md ruling 8 (lines 87-93) gives the decision to label a correction from α or ω; methods/scales.py:111-114 quotes the source.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_ms8_scales.py (line 526: assert any('omits transient error' in l for l in corr['labels']))
note: Code matches: TRANSIENT (core/scales.py:65-66) is attached to rc_internal_consistency's inference wording, and the methods sentence (core/scales.py:1008-1010) adds it when the correction comes from ω. The tests only check that the text is shown; no simulation with transient error checks the under-correction. Tier-1 effect: rc_test_retest is ranked 'recommended' and rc_internal_consistency 'available' (core/scales.py:128-145). The source supports the claim as stated, but only partly supports that ranking: by the same source, test-retest misses specific-factor error and is not the complete coefficient (CES is). The ranking should say so, or be framed as 'includes transient error, omits item-specific error'.

source_note: Both internal sources exist and say it: readings.py:19-24 lists 'no clustering without a confirmed unit' among the conservative paths, and BLUEPRINT.md §14.1 (lines 584-588) says 'the consumer asks, or takes the conservative path: no unit in the sentence, no clustering without a confirmed unit'. Both give only a decision. 'Conservative' there means the recognition leash (a guessed reading must never change a number unasked), not statistical conservatism, and no methods reason is given for the direction. For held-out and cross-validated scores, splitting a unit's rows across train and test is the optimistic direction (the standard result on blocked CV for dependent data, e.g. Roberts et al. 2017, Ecography; not cited here). So the basis does not support 'conservative' in the statistical sense.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_recognition_leash.py (line 972: basis.state == 'abandoned' and 'awaits its own confirmation'); turbotab/core/tests/acceptance/test_readings_ledger.py (line 533: grouped_by is None)
note: Code matches: split_inputs groups only by an identifier whose cluster reading is settled 'yes' (stages/rows.py:1949-1975), and seal.decide_basis never groups by an unconfirmed identifier (seal.py:209-219). The tests pin that behavior; none tests the direction of the bias. What decide_basis shows: when the grain is 'repeated' and only an unconfirmed identifier repeats, the basis is 'abandoned' with 'its identifier role awaits its own confirmation, so the held-out rows were drawn by row. A unit can sit on both sides: treat held-out scores as exploratory.' (seal.py:271-277). Under 'one row per unit' with an unconfirmed repeat, the basis is also 'abandoned' and says to treat held-out scores as exploratory (seal.py:283-291). So the seal discloses the optimism. The CV folds from split_inputs carry no such note: rows.py's fold sentence mentions grouping only when grouped. Under inference, resolve_clusters asks (CONSUMERS: ASK), which is the truly conservative path. Sent to review because, for the held-out draw and the folds, the label 'conservative' is backwards: it is the leash-safe path and is statistically optimistic. Either ask, as inference does, or keep the 'exploratory' disclosure and extend it to the CV scores.

corrected_statement: The injection order and the analytical batch along which QC-RLSC fits each feature's drift are never settled from the values: a sample number is also all-distinct, and a preparation plate or a study group run in blocks also forms contiguous blocks (KIND_RULES, no value test). The guesses are, for the order: a column named as a run order whose values are complete, distinct numbers (medium confidence), else a whole-number permutation of 1..n or 0..n-1 (low). For the batch: columns named batch, run or plate, in that order of trust, with 2+ levels, each level on 2+ rows and at most max(2, n/4) levels (medium); then, name-blind, any non-float column meeting the same level rules whose levels each occupy one unbroken stretch of the injection order (low). At most two batch candidates are offered beside 'one curve over the whole run', and the user's choice settles them.
source_note: KIND_RULES injection_order and batch (readings.py:1305-1313, :1330-1337) state the alternatives and 'settled_by' the user's choice. METABOLOMICS_PACK.md §01 (docs/turbotab-next/reference/research/, lines 54-56, 74-78) rules that the tool 'must never guess silently. Present the inference with its evidence and require confirmation' [SETTLED], and lists run-order and batch names (injection.order, run_order, sequence, acq_order, batch, plate). The pack does not describe the permutation-of-rows or contiguous-block heuristics, or the cap of two; those are the app's own (the MS7 repair). These are decisions, with the alternatives as the reason values cannot settle the readings.
note: test_2a checks the structure: each option names its order and batch column, KIND_RULES has no value test and is settled by the user, and the consumers are registered. It is behavior and text, and it never calls injection_order_reading or batch_readings with the permutation, block or cap cases (no test references them directly). test_2b is a known-truth simulation showing that per-batch correction beats one curve when batch offsets exist (median SD at most 0.065 against worse). That shows why the batch reading matters, not that the guesses are right. The statement's 'else' for the block reading is wrong: block candidates are added after named ones and can fill the second slot. The level cap is max(2, n//4), not n/4. The claim is a reasoned recognition design, and asking the user is its safeguard.

source_note: No source is attached to the qrilc_under_inference refusal (omics.py:1471-1478) or its contract option (omics.py:1891-1893, 'Refused: one draw outside the multiple imputation'). The principle that a single imputation treated as observed understates variance is textbook (Rubin 1987; Little & Rubin), and it is the reasoning Lubin et al. 2004 use for detection limits. LUBIN is cited for the neighboring refusals, not this one. QRILC's own sources (Lazar et al. 2016; Wei et al. 2018, omics.py:1107-1138) are about its point accuracy, not inference.
note: Code matches: under inference, below_detection == 'qrilc' raises the refusal with the censored-normal-within-MI exit. test_4c only asserts the refusal code, i.e. the behavior; no simulation compares interval coverage of a QRILC single fill with the censored-normal draw within MI. test_4d checks QRILC's point recovery only. Sent to review because the rule is applied unevenly. Half the minimum is also one fill outside the multiple imputation (a constant, so it carries even less uncertainty), yet under inference it is accepted at <= 10% censored and with attestation above (omics.py:1480-1492; test_4c line 590). Either the uncertainty reason also covers half-minimum, with its acceptance resting on Lubin's small-bias-at-low-share argument (a bias argument, not a variance one), or QRILC deserves the same 'customary at this share, recorded' path. The stated reason is sound; its application is not consistent.

source_note: No source at coach.py:492-495. The underlying identity, that the variance of the mean of k independent, equal-variance errors is sigma_w^2/k, is elementary and holds only under those assumptions. The app's own teaching content contradicts them for the common case: teaching/content.py:557-561 ('Recalls on consecutive days have correlated errors, so within-person variation is underestimated', SETTLED, NUT03). With positively correlated replicate errors the reduction is smaller than k-fold.
test_judged: turbotab/core/tests/test_coach.py (line 143: assert texts == ['Averaging `2` replicates cuts within-person variance `2`-fold.'])
note: Code matches: when the aggregation is 'mean', the median rows per unit k >= 2 and the repeat kind is 'repeats', the note says 'Averaging k replicates cuts within-person variance k-fold' (coach.py:491-494). The test checks only the text. Three imprecisions: (1) what shrinks is the error variance of each person's mean, not 'within-person variance' itself; (2) k is the median count, so units with fewer rows gain less; (3) the k-fold factor needs independent, equal-variance replicate errors, which the app says fails for consecutive-day recalls. Suggested wording: 'Averaging `k` replicates divides the day-to-day error in each person's mean by up to `k` (fully when the replicates' errors are independent).'

source_note: WHAT_EXPLORATION_MAY_DECIDE.md (docs/turbotab-next/understanding/research/, §4.2 lines 121-125) says 'missingness that piles up at low intensity means left-censored data, missing not at random' and cites Wei 2018 and Yang 2015. Wei R et al., Sci Rep 2018;8:663 (doi 10.1038/s41598-017-19120-0, PMC5766532) was verified on Europe PMC with its full text. It treats values under the LOQ as left-censored MNAR and diagnoses abundance dependence ('missing values were abundance-dependent since response values of missing part are significantly lower than the non-missing part'). It also names other preprocessing causes: peak picking of low signal-to-noise compounds, deconvolution, and alignment with retention-time shifts. Yang 2015 was not verified; it is likely Yang et al., Front Mol Biosci, the modified 80% rule, which the line cites for the filter. METABOLOMICS_PACK.md §03 (lines 222-225) gives the diagnostic: a strong negative relation between missing rate and intensity means left-censoring/MNAR, and a flat one means MCAR/MAR from peak-picking or alignment failure.
note: Code matches: packs._left_censored (turbotab/packs.py:625-675) fires when Spearman rho(missing rate, log mean observed abundance) <= -0.5 over at least 30 positive-mean features with at least 5 having blanks. finding_words.py:802-808 gives the user line and routes to the non-detection fill. The tests check that it fires on a fixture built to be left-censored (rho < -0.9) and not on a zero-filled export. No test checks that it stays silent under MCAR/MAR missingness, and none could check the inference itself. The inventory's caveat is fair and Wei 2018 says so too: low-abundance features also fail peak picking more often, which is still intensity-dependent. So 'likely below detection' is the right hedge. 'Not missing at random' is the MNAR reading the sources give. A low-S/N peak-picking failure is arguably MNAR too, but not a value below a fixed limit.

corrected_statement: Under inference, rows that are imputed copies of one record (e.g., NHANES DXA's five imputations) are each analyzed as a completed dataset with their own outcome, and the estimates are pooled by Rubin's rules. This happens when the column numbering the copies is named and each copy is kept as a record (set_unit 'row'; stages/modeling.py:1462-1472). Combining the copies into one row per unit is blocked unless recorded as a limitation. The methods sentence (voice.py:2085-2088) states the pooling whenever the answer is not acknowledged, even before those two conditions hold. The teaching card (teaching/content.py:541-543) says instead that under inference the copies are 'kept only as a recorded limitation'.
source_note: The contract cites 'NCHS, NHANES DXA multiple imputation data files (2008)' and 'Rubin 1987' (methods/missing.py:1977). The NCHS DXA page (wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Nhanes/Dxa/Dxa.aspx, fetched) says: 'The preferred statistical approach is to analyze EACH OF THE FIVE datasets separately using methods and software that are appropriate for survey data and then combining the estimates and standard errors using the combining rules', and 'The extra variability due to imputation CANNOT be incorporated by simply analyzing a SINGLE dataset as if the imputed values were true values' (quoted at structural.py:571). It supports the claim in this regime. NCHS's own direction adds survey-appropriate methods for each copy. 'MS3' is the internal package (MODELING_SEQUENCE).
note: The R test fits lm per copy with HC3 in R and pools with mitools::MIcombine and mice::pool.scalar. It matches the engine's pooled coefficients and total variances to 1e-6 and the df and interval to 1e-4: an independent reference that would fail if the copies were not pooled by Rubin's rules. That Rubin's rules carry the imputation uncertainty assumes the provider's imputation was proper and congenial with this analysis model. This is not stated, and is not checkable here. Sent to review for two inconsistencies in what the app tells the user. (1) The teaching option text 'under inference kept only as a recorded limitation' (content.py:541-543) contradicts the fit and the methods sentence. (2) voice.py:2085-2088 asserts pooling under inference without checking implicate_column or unit == 'row'. imputed_copies_column returns None, so nothing is pooled, when the copy column is not named or the unit is not yet answered.

corrected_statement: The design docs rule that Results wording starts at the design's floor: an association for an observational design. 'An estimated effect, its assumptions named' is offered only under Estimate, with the estimand declared and the unmeasured-confounding exhibit beside it, and only when no standing question points elsewhere and no stated assumption is refuted (the last clause from BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md:683, not FOUNDATION). Causal wording is offered only for trials, and model explanations are never worded as effects. The drafted wordings with claim strengths, 'Write my own', and the noticing on stronger user wording are planned (SIZING C7a, listed under 'Next' in HANDOFF.md:136) and not yet in the engine. What the code enforces today: causal wording only for a trial's intention-to-treat set (methods/trials.py:92-95, trial_sentence); explanations and adjustment terms labeled 'not an effect estimate' (models/explain.py:84, :1705, :1724; stages/effects.py:1684); the observational design's option text 'results are worded as associations' (teaching/content.py:411); and the causal lane's methods sentence, worded as an estimated effect resting on the declared assumptions.
source_note: The internal rulings exist: calm/FOUNDATION.md §8 (lines 456-479, the floor 'as the orchestrator's methods floor of 2026-10-06') lists the claim strengths and 'explanations are never worded as effects; causal wording is offered only for trials'. BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md:681-684 adds 'only when no question points elsewhere and no stated assumption is refuted'. CROSSWALK.md:1476 and :1538-1544 give the draft templates. These are decisions with brief reasons (curation must not become selective reporting). No external source is cited for the wording levels.
note: No engine or frontend code drafts Results wordings by claim strength or raises a noticing on stronger user wording: searches for 'assumptions named', 'Write my own' and claim-strength names find only docs. So 'app_action: refuses' describes planned behavior. The trial test checks only that the ITT sentence uses causal wording and the per-protocol one does not. The inventory's tension with the causal lane (DML/TMLE) is resolved in the docs themselves: FOUNDATION keeps 'estimated effect with its assumptions named' as its own level, distinct from 'causal (trials only)', and the causal lane's methods sentence ('The total effect ... was also estimated ... It rests on the declared assumptions of no unmeasured confounding ...', test_causal_lane.py test_9) is that level. Sent to review because the ledger should not present this as a shipped refusal until C7a lands; once built, it needs a test that a stronger user wording raises the noticing.
